terms.gloss: neither hot nor cold: at room temperature
evidence: Sen. Ep. 67.1: nec calidum nec frīgidum patī
terms.comment: A description, in Seneca’s words: writing of the cool spring, he says he still takes the chill off his bath water, which his friend calls putting up with “nothing hot or cold”. No reference work we searched (Traupman, Morgan–Owens, Levi–Bini) has a phrase for room temperature. Of water warmed a little, see “lukewarm”.

phrases.latin: Aquam mihi dā nec calidam nec frīgidam, quaesō.
phrases.english: Give me water at room temperature, please.

phrases.latin: nōndum mē committō frīgidae vērae, adhūc rigōrem ejus īnfringō. «Hoc est» inquis «nec calidum nec frīgidum patī.»
phrases.english: I don’t yet trust myself to really cold water; I still take the edge off its chill. “That means,” you say, “putting up with nothing either hot or cold.”

sources: Lewis & Short: calidus · Lewis & Short: frigidus
